title: Intake Camshaft Timing Over-Advanced (Bank 1)
plain_english: The engine computer cannot get the intake cam timing where it wants it. This is usually an oil or oil-control problem, not a broken engine.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but check the oil level first and fix it soon.
next_checks: check oil level and condition
change the oil if it is overdue
test or swap the oil control solenoid
misdiagnosis_notes: Start with an oil change and the solenoid. Do not jump straight to timing chain or phaser replacement.
high_mileage_note: Past 100k miles a stretched timing chain becomes a more realistic cause, especially with rattling on cold start.

title: Exhaust Camshaft Timing Over-Advanced (Bank 1)
plain_english: The exhaust cam timing is not where the engine computer commanded it. It is most often caused by oil condition or the oil control solenoid.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but check the oil level first and fix it soon.
next_checks: check oil level and condition
change the oil if it is overdue
test or swap the exhaust oil control solenoid
misdiagnosis_notes: Rule out low or old oil and the solenoid before paying for timing components.
high_mileage_note: Past 100k miles timing chain stretch is more likely, especially if the oil has not been changed regularly.

title: Crankshaft/Camshaft Position Correlation (Bank 1 Sensor A)
plain_english: The crankshaft and camshaft are not lined up the way the computer expects. That can mean a timing problem inside the engine.
safe_to_drive: Drive as little as possible. If the engine rattles, runs rough, or is hard to start, do not drive it.
common_causes: stretched timing chain or worn tensioner
sticking cam phaser or oil control solenoid
next_checks: check oil level and condition
listen for chain rattle on cold start
have cam/crank correlation checked with a scan tool
misdiagnosis_notes: Replacing only a sensor often does not fix this. The mechanical timing should be verified.
high_mileage_note: On a high-mileage engine a stretched timing chain is the leading suspect.

title: Fuel Rail/System Pressure Too Low
plain_english: The engine is not getting enough fuel pressure. It may hesitate, lose power, or stall.
safe_to_drive: Not recommended. The engine can lose power or stall without warning.
common_causes: faulty fuel pressure sensor or regulator
next_checks: look and smell for fuel leaks
measure fuel pressure with a gauge
check when the fuel filter was last replaced
misdiagnosis_notes: Measure the actual fuel pressure before replacing the pump. A cheap filter or sensor can cause the same code.

title: Mass Air Flow (MAF) Sensor Range/Performance
plain_english: The sensor that measures air entering the engine is reporting numbers that do not make sense.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes, but expect poor fuel economy, hesitation, or rough idle until it is fixed.
common_causes: dirty or badly seated air filter
air leak between the MAF and the engine
next_checks: inspect the air filter and intake tube
clean the MAF with MAF sensor cleaner only
look for cracked intake hoses
misdiagnosis_notes: Cleaning the sensor and fixing intake leaks solves this more often than a new sensor does.

title: Mass Air Flow (MAF) Sensor Circuit Low Input
plain_english: The air flow sensor is sending a signal that is too low, or no signal at all.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes, but the engine may run poorly or stall.
next_checks: make sure the MAF connector is fully plugged in
inspect the wiring for damage
clean the sensor with MAF cleaner
misdiagnosis_notes: This often appears right after an air filter change when the connector was left loose.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor Circuit High Input
plain_english: The sensor that reads incoming air temperature is reporting an impossible value, usually because it is unplugged or the wiring is open.
safe_to_drive: Yes. Fuel economy and cold starts may be slightly worse.
next_checks: check that the sensor and MAF connectors are plugged in
inspect the wiring and connector pins
misdiagnosis_notes: On many cars this sensor is built into the MAF sensor. Check the connector before buying parts.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit High Input
plain_english: The coolant temperature sensor is reporting an impossibly cold engine, usually from a bad connection or failed sensor.
safe_to_drive: Short trips only, and watch the temperature gauge. The cooling fans and fuel mixture may not behave correctly.
next_checks: check the coolant level with the engine cold
inspect the sensor connector
compare the scan tool temperature reading to reality
misdiagnosis_notes: Never open a hot radiator cap. Check the connector and coolant level before replacing the sensor.

title: Throttle Position Sensor Range/Performance
plain_english: The sensor that tells the computer how far the throttle is open is giving readings that do not match what the engine is doing.
safe_to_drive: With caution. The car may hesitate, surge, or go into reduced-power mode.
next_checks: clean the throttle body
inspect the connector and wiring
watch the throttle position reading on a scan tool
misdiagnosis_notes: A throttle body cleaning fixes many of these. Do not force an electronic throttle plate open by hand.

title: Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature
plain_english: The engine is staying cooler than it should, or taking too long to warm up.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes, but repair soon. The heater may be weak and fuel economy drops.
next_checks: check the coolant level with the engine cold
watch how long the engine takes to reach normal temperature
check live coolant temperature on a scan tool
misdiagnosis_notes: Check thermostat behavior and coolant level before replacing the sensor.

title: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
plain_english: The front oxygen sensor is reading very lean or its signal is stuck low.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for now, but fix it soon to protect the catalytic converter.
common_causes: vacuum leak making the engine run lean
next_checks: listen for exhaust leaks near the manifold
check for other lean codes like P0171
inspect the sensor wiring
misdiagnosis_notes: If lean codes are also present, the sensor may be telling the truth. Find the lean cause first.

title: O2 Sensor Slow Response (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
plain_english: The front oxygen sensor is reacting too slowly, which usually means it is worn out.
safe_to_drive: Yes, but fuel economy may suffer. Fix it when convenient.
common_causes: contaminated sensor from coolant or oil burning
next_checks: check the age and mileage of the sensor
listen for exhaust leaks
check for oil or coolant consumption
misdiagnosis_notes: Use a quality sensor. Cheap universal sensors often bring the code back.
high_mileage_note: Oxygen sensors commonly wear out around 100k miles, so simple age is the most likely cause here.

title: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Malfunction (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
plain_english: The built-in heater that warms up the front oxygen sensor is not working.
safe_to_drive: Yes. Emissions and fuel economy are slightly worse until it is fixed.
common_causes: burned-out heater inside the oxygen sensor
next_checks: check the O2 heater fuse
inspect the sensor wiring for melting or chafing
measure the heater resistance
misdiagnosis_notes: Check the fuse first. If the fuse is good, the sensor itself is the usual fix.

title: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Malfunction (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
plain_english: The heater in the rear oxygen sensor, the one after the catalytic converter, is not working.
safe_to_drive: Yes. It mainly affects emissions monitoring.
common_causes: burned-out heater inside the rear oxygen sensor
next_checks: check the O2 heater fuse
inspect the wiring under the car for damage
measure the heater resistance
misdiagnosis_notes: This is the downstream sensor. Make sure the correct sensor is replaced.

title: System Too Lean (Bank 1)
plain_english: The engine is getting too much air or not enough fuel.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but fix it soon. Running lean for a long time can damage the engine or catalytic converter.
common_causes: weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter
leaking intake gasket or PCV hose
exhaust leak before the oxygen sensor
next_checks: listen for hissing vacuum leaks with the engine running
inspect intake and PCV hoses for cracks
clean the MAF sensor
check fuel pressure
misdiagnosis_notes: Do not replace oxygen sensors for this code. They are usually reporting a real lean condition.
high_mileage_note: On a high-mileage car, hardened rubber vacuum and PCV hoses and a tired fuel pump become more likely.

title: System Too Rich (Bank 1)
plain_english: The engine is getting too much fuel or not enough air.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but fix it soon. Extra fuel can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter.
common_causes: high fuel pressure from a bad regulator
next_checks: inspect the air filter
clean the MAF sensor
check for fuel smell in the engine oil
check fuel pressure
misdiagnosis_notes: Do not start with oxygen sensors. Look for the reason the engine is actually running rich.

title: System Too Lean (Bank 2)
plain_english: The second side of the engine is getting too much air or not enough fuel.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but fix it soon.
common_causes: weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter
next_checks: listen for hissing vacuum leaks
clean the MAF sensor
check whether P0171 is also set
check fuel pressure
misdiagnosis_notes: If P0171 and P0174 appear together, suspect something shared by both sides: the MAF sensor, fuel pressure, or a large vacuum leak.

title: System Too Rich (Bank 2)
plain_english: The second side of the engine is getting too much fuel or not enough air.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but fix it soon to protect the catalytic converter.
next_checks: inspect the air filter
clean the MAF sensor
check whether P0172 is also set
check fuel pressure
misdiagnosis_notes: If both banks are rich, look at shared parts such as the MAF sensor and fuel pressure regulator first.

title: Injector Circuit Malfunction (Cylinder 1)
plain_english: The electrical circuit for the cylinder 1 fuel injector has a problem, so that cylinder may not be getting fuel correctly.
safe_to_drive: Drive as little as possible. A dead cylinder causes misfires that can damage the catalytic converter.
next_checks: inspect the injector connector and wiring
listen for the injector clicking
measure injector resistance and compare with the others
misdiagnosis_notes: This is an electrical code. Check the wiring and connector before replacing the injector.

title: Engine Overheat Condition
plain_english: The engine got dangerously hot.
safe_to_drive: No. Pull over safely and shut the engine off. Driving an overheating engine can destroy it.
next_checks: let the engine cool completely before touching anything
check the coolant level when cold
look for coolant leaks under the car
check that the radiator fans run
misdiagnosis_notes: Never open the radiator cap on a hot engine. Find why it overheated before simply topping up coolant.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Underboost
plain_english: The turbo is not making as much boost pressure as the engine computer asked for, so the car feels weak.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes, gently. Avoid hard acceleration until it is checked.
common_causes: boost leak from a loose or split hose
next_checks: inspect intercooler and boost hoses and clamps
check the air filter
listen for whooshing or whining under acceleration
misdiagnosis_notes: Most underboost codes are leaks or control parts, not a dead turbo. Pressure-test the intake before replacing the turbocharger.

title: Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected
plain_english: The engine is stumbling. One or more cylinders are not firing correctly.
safe_to_drive: Drive as little as possible. If the check engine light is flashing, stop driving: raw fuel is overheating the catalytic converter.
next_checks: inspect the spark plugs
check the ignition coils
look for vacuum leaks
check fuel pressure
misdiagnosis_notes: Do not assume spark plugs only. Fuel delivery or mechanical problems can also cause this.
high_mileage_note: If the spark plugs have never been changed on a high-mileage engine, they are the first thing to check.

title: Cylinder 1 Misfire Detected
plain_english: Cylinder number 1 is not firing correctly, so the engine runs rough or shakes.
safe_to_drive: Drive as little as possible. If the check engine light is flashing, stop driving.
next_checks: swap the cylinder 1 coil with another cylinder and see if the misfire moves
inspect the cylinder 1 spark plug
check the injector connector
misdiagnosis_notes: Swap-test the coil before buying one. If the misfire stays on cylinder 1 after swapping coil and plug, look at the injector or compression.
high_mileage_note: On a high-mileage engine, original spark plugs and coils are the most likely cause.

title: Cylinder 2 Misfire Detected
plain_english: Cylinder number 2 is not firing correctly, so the engine runs rough or shakes.
safe_to_drive: Drive as little as possible. If the check engine light is flashing, stop driving.
next_checks: swap the cylinder 2 coil with another cylinder and see if the misfire moves
inspect the cylinder 2 spark plug
check the injector connector
misdiagnosis_notes: Swap-test the coil before buying one. If the misfire stays on cylinder 2 after swapping coil and plug, look at the injector or compression.
high_mileage_note: On a high-mileage engine, original spark plugs and coils are the most likely cause.

title: Cylinder 3 Misfire Detected
plain_english: Cylinder number 3 is not firing correctly, so the engine runs rough or shakes.
safe_to_drive: Drive as little as possible. If the check engine light is flashing, stop driving.
next_checks: swap the cylinder 3 coil with another cylinder and see if the misfire moves
inspect the cylinder 3 spark plug
check the injector connector
misdiagnosis_notes: Swap-test the coil before buying one. If the misfire stays on cylinder 3 after swapping coil and plug, look at the injector or compression.
high_mileage_note: On a high-mileage engine, original spark plugs and coils are the most likely cause.

title: Cylinder 4 Misfire Detected
plain_english: Cylinder number 4 is not firing correctly, so the engine runs rough or shakes.
safe_to_drive: Drive as little as possible. If the check engine light is flashing, stop driving.
next_checks: swap the cylinder 4 coil with another cylinder and see if the misfire moves
inspect the cylinder 4 spark plug
check the injector connector
misdiagnosis_notes: Swap-test the coil before buying one. If the misfire stays on cylinder 4 after swapping coil and plug, look at the injector or compression.
high_mileage_note: On a high-mileage engine, original spark plugs and coils are the most likely cause.

title: Knock Sensor 1 Circuit Malfunction (Bank 1)
plain_english: The sensor that listens for engine knock is not sending a usable signal.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes, gently. The engine may feel weaker because the computer plays it safe with ignition timing.
next_checks: inspect the knock sensor wiring and connector
check for rodent damage to the harness
measure the sensor resistance
misdiagnosis_notes: Wiring faults are common here. On some engines the sensor sits under the intake manifold, so confirm the fault before paying for that labor.

title: Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Malfunction
plain_english: The computer is not getting a good signal from the sensor that tracks engine rotation.
safe_to_drive: Not recommended. The engine can stall suddenly or refuse to restart.
common_causes: oil or metal debris on the sensor tip
next_checks: inspect the sensor connector and wiring
check whether the tachometer moves while cranking
inspect the sensor tip for debris
misdiagnosis_notes: Check the wiring and connector first. A sensor that fails only when hot is a classic pattern.

title: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Malfunction (Bank 1)
plain_english: The computer is not getting a good signal from the camshaft position sensor.
safe_to_drive: With caution and only short trips. Expect hard starting, stalling, or rough running.
next_checks: inspect the sensor connector for oil or corrosion
inspect the wiring
check for timing-related codes like P0016
misdiagnosis_notes: If the code returns with a new sensor, check the wiring and the mechanical timing.

title: Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) Flow Insufficient
plain_english: Not enough exhaust gas is flowing back into the engine through the EGR system, usually because it is clogged with carbon.
safe_to_drive: Yes. You may notice pinging under load, and the car can fail an emissions test.
common_causes: faulty EGR pressure or position sensor
next_checks: inspect and clean the EGR valve and passages
check vacuum hoses to the EGR system
test the EGR valve with a scan tool
misdiagnosis_notes: Clogged passages are more common than a bad valve. A new valve on a clogged passage will not fix it.
high_mileage_note: Carbon buildup in the EGR passages is very common on high-mileage engines.

title: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)
plain_english: The exhaust system is not cleaning emissions as well as it should.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but fix it soon.
next_checks: check for misfire or fuel trim codes first
inspect for exhaust leaks
compare upstream and downstream O2 sensor readings
misdiagnosis_notes: Check O2 sensors and exhaust leaks before replacing the catalytic converter. Fix any misfires first or a new converter will fail too.
high_mileage_note: Past 100k miles a genuinely worn-out catalytic converter is the most likely cause, but still rule out the cheaper items first.

title: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)
plain_english: The catalytic converter on the second side of the engine is not cleaning the exhaust as well as it should.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but fix it soon.
next_checks: check for misfire or fuel trim codes first
inspect for exhaust leaks
compare upstream and downstream O2 sensor readings
misdiagnosis_notes: Check O2 sensors and exhaust leaks before replacing the catalytic converter.
high_mileage_note: Past 100k miles a genuinely worn-out catalytic converter is the most likely cause, but still rule out the cheaper items first.

title: Evaporative Emission (EVAP) System Malfunction
plain_english: The system that traps gasoline vapors from the fuel tank has a fault.
safe_to_drive: Yes. It does not affect how the car drives, but it should be fixed for emissions.
next_checks: tighten the gas cap until it clicks and inspect its seal
inspect visible EVAP hoses
have a smoke test done if the code returns
misdiagnosis_notes: Start with the gas cap. A smoke test finds the real leak faster than guessing at parts.

title: EVAP System Incorrect Purge Flow
plain_english: Fuel vapors are not being drawn into the engine the way the computer expects.
safe_to_drive: Yes. Fix it when convenient.
next_checks: check the gas cap
inspect the purge valve hoses
test the purge valve
misdiagnosis_notes: The purge valve is the usual culprit, but check the hoses to it first.

title: EVAP System Leak Detected (Small Leak)
plain_english: There is a small leak in the system that traps fuel vapors.
safe_to_drive: Yes. It does not affect how the car drives.
common_causes: small crack in the filler neck or canister
next_checks: tighten the gas cap until it clicks
inspect the gas cap seal for cracks
have a smoke test done if the code returns
misdiagnosis_notes: Replace a worn gas cap first. Small leaks are hard to see, and a smoke test is the reliable way to find them.

title: EVAP Vent Control Circuit Malfunction
plain_english: The valve that lets fresh air into the fuel vapor system is not working correctly.
safe_to_drive: Yes. You may have trouble filling the tank, with the pump clicking off early.
next_checks: inspect the vent valve near the charcoal canister for dirt or blockage
check the wiring and connector
check the gas cap
misdiagnosis_notes: Dirt and spider nests in the vent are common. Avoid topping off the tank after the pump clicks off, since it floods the canister.

title: EVAP System Leak Detected (Large Leak)
plain_english: There is a large leak in the system that traps fuel vapors. Very often the gas cap is loose or missing.
safe_to_drive: Yes. You may smell fuel, and it should be fixed for emissions.
common_causes: loose, missing, or damaged gas cap
next_checks: check that the gas cap is present and tight
inspect EVAP hoses for disconnections
have a smoke test done if the code returns
misdiagnosis_notes: Check the gas cap before anything else. After tightening it, the light can take a few days of driving to clear.

title: EVAP System Leak Detected (Very Small Leak)
plain_english: There is a very small leak in the system that traps fuel vapors.
safe_to_drive: Yes. It does not affect how the car drives.
common_causes: tiny crack in an EVAP hose
next_checks: inspect and tighten the gas cap
replace the gas cap if the seal is hardened
have a smoke test done if the code returns
misdiagnosis_notes: These leaks are tiny. Do not buy parts without a smoke test unless the gas cap is clearly worn.

title: EVAP System Leak Detected (Fuel Cap Loose/Off)
plain_english: The car thinks the gas cap is loose or missing.
safe_to_drive: Yes.
common_causes: gas cap left loose or off after refueling
next_checks: tighten the gas cap until it clicks
inspect the gas cap seal
drive for a few days and see if the light clears
misdiagnosis_notes: This is almost always the cap. Give it several drive cycles to clear before doing anything else.

title: Vehicle Speed Sensor Malfunction
plain_english: The computer is not getting a reliable vehicle speed signal.
safe_to_drive: With caution. The speedometer, cruise control, or transmission shifting may misbehave.
common_causes: failed wheel speed sensor on cars that use ABS for speed
next_checks: check whether the speedometer works
check for ABS codes
inspect the speed sensor wiring
misdiagnosis_notes: Many newer cars get speed from the ABS wheel sensors, so read ABS codes before replacing a transmission speed sensor.

title: Idle Air Control System Malfunction
plain_english: The engine cannot hold a steady idle speed.
safe_to_drive: With caution. The engine may stall at stops or idle too high.
common_causes: dirty or failed idle air control valve
next_checks: clean the throttle body
listen for vacuum leaks
clean or test the idle air control valve
misdiagnosis_notes: Clean the throttle body and check for vacuum leaks before replacing the idle control valve.

title: Idle Control System RPM Lower Than Expected
plain_english: The engine is idling slower than the computer wants.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes, but it may stall at stops.
next_checks: clean the throttle body
inspect the air filter
check for other codes
misdiagnosis_notes: A throttle body cleaning fixes most of these. Some cars need an idle relearn procedure afterward.

title: Idle Control System RPM Higher Than Expected
plain_english: The engine is idling faster than the computer wants.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes. The car may creep forward more than normal, so brake firmly.
common_causes: leaking intake gasket or PCV valve
next_checks: listen for hissing vacuum leaks
inspect the PCV valve and hoses
clean the throttle body
misdiagnosis_notes: A high idle is extra air getting in somewhere. Find the leak before replacing parts.

title: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor Range/Performance
plain_english: The oil pressure reading does not make sense to the engine computer. It may be a bad sensor, or oil pressure may really be wrong.
safe_to_drive: Check the oil level before driving. If the red oil warning light is on or the engine is ticking or knocking, do not drive it.
common_causes: worn oil pump or clogged pickup (less common)
next_checks: check the oil level on the dipstick
check when the oil was last changed and what grade was used
have real oil pressure measured with a mechanical gauge
misdiagnosis_notes: The sensor is the usual fix, but verify actual oil pressure with a gauge. Assuming it is only the sensor can cost you an engine.

title: System Voltage Low
plain_english: The car's electrical system voltage is lower than it should be. The battery is not being charged properly.
safe_to_drive: Short trips only. The car can die and leave you stranded once the battery runs down.
next_checks: clean and tighten the battery terminals
inspect the drive belt
have the battery and alternator tested, which most parts stores do for free
misdiagnosis_notes: Have both the battery and alternator tested before buying either one.
high_mileage_note: An original alternator on a high-mileage car is a strong suspect.

title: Engine Control Module Processor Fault
plain_english: The engine computer has detected a problem with itself.
safe_to_drive: With caution. The car may run badly, shift strangely, or stall.
common_causes: poor computer ground or power connection
next_checks: have the battery and charging system tested
inspect the computer connectors and grounds for corrosion
ask a dealer whether a software update exists
misdiagnosis_notes: Rule out battery, ground, and software issues first. A replacement computer is expensive and usually needs programming.

title: Transmission Control System Malfunction
plain_english: The transmission computer has found a problem and asked for the check engine light. This code is only a flag, and the real fault is stored as another code.
safe_to_drive: With caution. If the transmission slips, bangs into gear, or is stuck in one gear, limit driving.
common_causes: a separate transmission fault code is stored
next_checks: read the transmission computer for the specific code
check the transmission fluid level and condition if there is a dipstick
misdiagnosis_notes: P0700 by itself tells you almost nothing. Get the actual transmission code before agreeing to any repair.

title: Transmission Input/Turbine Speed Sensor Circuit Malfunction
plain_english: The transmission is not getting a good signal from the sensor that measures its input speed.
safe_to_drive: With caution. Shifting may be harsh or the transmission may stay in one gear.
next_checks: check the transmission fluid level and condition
inspect the sensor connector and wiring
misdiagnosis_notes: Check the wiring and fluid first. On some transmissions the sensor is inside and costs more labor to reach.

title: Incorrect Gear Ratio
plain_english: The transmission is not in the gear the computer commanded, which usually means it is slipping.
safe_to_drive: Drive as little as possible. Continued driving on a slipping transmission makes the damage worse.
next_checks: check the transmission fluid level, color, and smell
note which gears slip or flare
have a transmission shop scan for related codes
misdiagnosis_notes: Low fluid can cause this by itself. Check the fluid before assuming the transmission needs a rebuild.
high_mileage_note: On a high-mileage transmission that has never had a fluid service, internal wear is more likely.

title: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Performance or Stuck Off
plain_english: The torque converter is not locking up at cruising speed the way it should.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips. Fuel economy drops and the transmission can run hotter, so avoid towing.
next_checks: check the transmission fluid level and condition
note whether engine RPM stays high at highway speed
have the lockup solenoid tested
misdiagnosis_notes: Check fluid and the solenoid before agreeing to a torque converter or transmission replacement.

title: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Lean (Bank 1)
plain_english: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter is seeing a lean exhaust.
safe_to_drive: Usually yes for short trips, but fix it soon.
common_causes: exhaust leak near the catalytic converter or sensors
next_checks: listen for exhaust leaks, especially on a cold start
check for other lean codes such as P0171
inspect the downstream O2 sensor wiring
misdiagnosis_notes: An exhaust leak is the most common cause. Do not replace the catalytic converter for this code alone.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor A/B Voltage Correlation
plain_english: The two sensors that track the throttle position disagree with each other, so the computer cannot trust them.
safe_to_drive: Not recommended. The car can suddenly drop into reduced-power mode in traffic.
common_causes: corroded or loose throttle body connector
next_checks: inspect the throttle body connector for corrosion or loose pins
inspect the wiring harness
check for manufacturer recalls or service bulletins
misdiagnosis_notes: Connector and wiring problems are common here. Inspect them before replacing the throttle body.

title: Lost Communication With Engine Control Module
plain_english: Other computers in the car cannot talk to the engine computer.
safe_to_drive: Not recommended. The engine may stall or refuse to start.
common_causes: blown fuse or bad relay for the engine computer
next_checks: have the battery tested and clean the terminals
check the engine computer fuses and relay
inspect grounds and connectors for corrosion
misdiagnosis_notes: Communication codes are very often caused by low battery voltage or a bad connection, not a dead computer.

title: Lost Communication With Transmission Control Module
plain_english: Other computers in the car cannot talk to the transmission computer.
safe_to_drive: With caution. The transmission may stay in one gear or shift harshly.
common_causes: blown fuse for the transmission computer
next_checks: have the battery tested and clean the terminals
check the transmission computer fuses
inspect the transmission connector for corrosion or fluid
misdiagnosis_notes: Check battery voltage, fuses, and connectors before condemning the transmission computer.
